body_markdown:
Late at night, deep in the recesses of some dark corner of the internet, I’ll spy a vintage vehicle many states away and gasp. *A diamond in the rough! I’ve done it. I’ve found it. I’m wise enough and sleuthy enough to have spotted it…*


There is no greater thrill in this world than buying a vintage car—and no faster way to ruin your judgment. That kind of magical thinking has gotten me into trouble a few times. Other times, it’s worked out.


I’ve been buying cars sight-unseen for 20 years. I started out doing things the right way: vetting the owner, having the vehicle inspected by a reputable mechanic before purchase, thoroughly scrutinizing the photos, and compiling as much historical information as possible on each car.


Eventually, after a few wins, my hubris outgrew my good sense. I slipped into believing the story I told myself was true: I had a unique gift for spotting gems from afar and that my previously deployed due diligence was unnecessary—a hindrance, even—to my obtaining said gem.


While living in Detroit a decade ago, I found a[Fiat 124](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/fiat/124/1970/1970-fiat-124-spider?id=aCn1I000000D4AtSAK) on Craigslist in Southern Illinois. It looked like a rare find; it had been owned for many years by a wealthy older Fiat aficionado. It didn’t have any rust or rust repair. And the seller talked the good talk and said the right things.


Stellantis


After haggling over the phone, I drove down to Illinois to tow it back one early spring weekend. Upon my arrival, the owner had it ready to go at the bottom of his driveway. He drove it up onto my auto transport before I could even get a look at it—before I’d even sat in it. This should have been my first warning sign.


When I got home, I finally inspected it. I found he’d poorly repainted some of the bodywork with spray paint not even close to the original color. The engine also fired up quickly and idled—even on cold, damp, Detroit spring mornings. But then it struggled to drive around the block—bucking, backfiring, and stalling.


Luckily, I had a friend who was a former attorney and who was especially irked by sellers who misrepresent their cars. So, he crafted a letter to the seller on my behalf, threatening legal action. Luckily for me, the old guy was scared by the letter and agreed to take the car back and return my money.


A few weeks later, after having humped the Fiat back to Illinois, I found a ’71 MGB in Indianapolis that I agreed to buy sight-unseen—again without inspection. It turned out to be a gem that I later sold for twice what I paid for it. That time, it worked out. I have a dozen or more stories like that. It’s really 50/50 on which way they split, gem or junker. *Sometimes you eat the bear, sometimes the bear eats you* .


If you are prepared to buy a car sight-unseen but aren’t particularly interested in fighting the proverbial bear for food-chain dominance, let me offer you some good habits to help navigate the process so you don’t get torched. Just don’t forget, even if you get a goodie, there will be[hidden costs with owning any collector car.](https://www.hagerty.com/media/advice/the-hidden-costs-of-owning-a-collector-vehicle/)


## The Buddy System


Bettmann Archive


My friends and I send each other vintage car listings on a daily basis, often believing we’ve found a gem. But the excitement of the find can obscure the vehicle’s flaws, which are readily apparent in the photos to an unbiased third party.


I’ve lost count of the number of times I’ve sent a listing to a friend with glee just to have him respond with a pithy one-liner about obvious rust or paint-color discrepancies. It goes both ways, of course, and I’ve highlighted pronounced condition issues for friends who were otherwise blind to them. This is why, now, my first line of defense against buying a junker is to send it to a keen-eyed friend.


If you don’t have such automotive compatriots, I recommend implementing a self-imposed cooldown period during which you go away from the listing for a bit before coming back to give it a second or third review.


Really look for telltale signs of ill repair: rust, dents, mismatched or discolored paint, and, if there are underbody shots, look for signs of fluid leaks.


Another thing to look for are missing components, especially under the hood. More often than not, this requires knowledge of the make or model in question and an understanding of what should be where. An image search for stock, correct examples can be a helpful guide, and spotting these kinds of things from listing photos can save you time and money down the road.


## Pre-Purchase Inspection


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Friends might say that I’ve wasted thousands of dollars on pre-purchase inspections (PPI). I’d counter by saying that I’ve *saved* thousands on cars because of PPI. From early ’60s Volvos to ’90s Land Cruisers to late-model BMWs, I’ve had all sorts of cars inspected; just because a collector car is 15 years old doesn’t mean it’s too new to be thoroughly looked over by an expert before purchase.


Before getting something 40 years old or older inspected, I recommend two things. One, try to find a specialty shop that knows what they’re looking at. Your average, generalized repair shop—especially now that we’re 40 years past the last time a carbureted car was sold new from the showroom floor—shouldn’t be relied upon to accurately assess a classic car’s condition. They might miss or misdiagnose plenty.


Second, keep an open mind and understand that no old car will be perfect. That was my approach with the[1991 Land Cruiser FJ80 I bought this spring](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/why-the-80-series-land-cruiser-is-the-most-notable-4x4-of-the-90s/) . Even low-mile examples will need stuff. You just have to decide in advance which stuff will be a dealbreaker. I told the Toyota specialists who looked at the FJ80 for me, “I don’t need you to go over it with a fine-toothed comb. I just want you to look for catastrophic or unsafe stuff.”


Even though that inspection came back with flying colors, the alternator failed 800 miles into my ownership. The alternator was fine until it wasn’t. And I didn’t expect a shop to identify that kind of thing.


## Red Flags


Wiki Commons/Kostas Goumagias


The first commandment of the sight-unseen buy in 2026: Ask for a video call. Not a video the seller made, a live one, where you direct the camera. Have them cold-start the car while you watch, walk the rockers, open the doors, pan the underside, inspect known problem areas. It costs nothing and takes ten minutes. A seller who won’t do that has a reason, and the reason is never good.


And a tell worth knowing: An old carbureted car that fires up too easily on your arrival has often been warmed up minutes before you got there. A genuine cold start is lumpy, reluctant. But don’t let a good start seduce you, either. That Fiat I mentioned started on the first crank every single time, stone cold, and it still couldn’t make it around the block without bucking and stalling. Starting and running are two different tests. Insist on seeing both.


Ask to see the title before any money moves. What you’re checking for: that it’s clean of brands, not a salvage, not rebuilt, not flooded, and that the VIN on the paper matches the VIN on the car. A mismatched VIN isn’t a negotiating point; it’s a walk-away. And if the title is signed by someone who isn’t the person you’re talking to, you’re buying from a flipper who skipped the paperwork. That alone isn’t a dealbreaker, but it tells you the seller’s history with the vehicle is measured in weeks, not years, so weigh any stories accordingly.


Treat the price as information. A rig priced well under market isn’t a windfall; it’s data. The local buyers got to see it in person, and they all passed. Ask yourself what they saw. Distance is the flipper’s best friend, because the sight-unseen buyer is the only one who can’t catch what every hometown tire-kicker already did.


While you’re at it, spend two minutes searching the phone number and the VIN. The same truck listed in another state, under another story, at another price, tells you everything.


Finally, beware the rushed close. The wire-today pressure, the phantom other buyer coming this afternoon, the old man hustling a Fiat onto your trailer before your truck is even in park. Urgency is always manufactured, and it’s manufactured for a reason.


Broadly speaking, look and listen for inconsistencies. Ask a lot of questions, request extra photos and video, ask for documentation, and if none exists, ask why. A seller above board won’t be offended by any of it. Some folks might advise you that if a car has had any paint or bodywork, it’s a dealbreaker. To me that’s unrealistic. Accidents happen. Done correctly, a moderate amount of paint work is totally acceptable. But again, ask for documentation.


## Getting It Home


Nick Jaynes


I’ve had vehicles shipped to my door that I’ve never seen in the metal. I’ve flown out and driven others home. I’ve driven out and towed dozens of vehicles home with me. Each has its own benefits and drawbacks.


Shipping can be a really easy way to get your sight-unseen car to your driveway. That is, so long as you do your homework finding a[reputable shipping company](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/car-shipping-is-complicated-thieves-are-taking-advantage/) and you’re not in a hurry to get it quickly. Auto shipping is maybe the most prime example in this world of getting what you pay for.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


I used to prefer to drive new-to-me vehicles home. The thrill of maybe not making it was part of the allure. As I’ve gotten older, though, I’d rather not add that level of drama to the already-risky endeavor of buying a vintage vehicle sight-unseen. So, now I’m inclined to drive my pickup truck out, snag an auto transport from U-Haul along the way, and drag it back.


The tow-it-home strategy isn’t perfect, either, of course. I’ve had hitch balls come loose, transfer-case linkages fail during dolly loading, death wobble, and transport tire blow-outs. These aren’t ideal. However, I’d still prefer to be in my modern heavy-duty truck during a freeway catastrophe than in a ’71 MGB.


## Conclusion


Getty Images


You’re never going to get the full story. Full stop. People never sell perfect cars. They’re going to tell you the rosiest version of the truth, or, if they’ve owned a car for decades, the truth they remember. Just know that going in.


I don’t want you to *not* buy cars sight-unseen. It’s a rush unlike virtually anything else in the car-collecting world, save vintage racing.


I am not a traditional adrenaline junkie; I have no desire to be hurled out of a plane or pushed off a bridge with a bungee rope around my ankles. Nor will I be heliskiing in this lifetime. But if you have a slightly suspect V-4–powered Saab you’d like to sell me, say no more. I am already grabbing the keys to my Ram and calling U-Haul.
